finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token to the user-supplied token with loose equality (==). An attacker who knows a victim's email can bypass the token check and set a new password for that account. Examples: a JSON boolean true (true == 'anystring' in PHP), integer 0 on PHP < 8, or a '0e...' magic-hash string when the stored token is also a numeric-looking string.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled $email and $token arguments, e.g. from a password-reset request body. A JSON-decoded body can give $token a bool or int type.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... at reset.php:5-6 (account password overwrite).

trace.note: Fetches the stored token for the attacker-chosen email.
$row['token'] == $token uses a type-juggling comparison, so true or 0 can match a non-empty token. The comparison is not constant-time either.
The victim's password hash is replaced with the attacker's chosen password, giving account takeover.

finding.guards_checked: Only the loose comparison guards the update. There is no type check on $token, no attempt limiting, and no expiry check. The sibling reset_password() at line 14 uses hash_equals with a (string) cast and is not affected. I did not find any caller of reset_password_loose in the repo, so exploitability depends on it being wired to a request handler. SQL injection is not possible because both values go through $db->quote().

verdict.guard_found: none (only the loose == comparison at reset.php:4; $db->quote() prevents SQLi but not the token bypass; no callers in repo, so reachability depends on wiring)
verdict.reason: reset.php:4 uses `$row['token'] == $token` with no type cast, so a JSON true (or a 0e magic hash) matches a stored token and reaches the password UPDATE at reset.php:5-6 for an anonymous attacker who knows the email; the function has no callers in the repo, so exploitability depends on it being wired to a request handler.

finding.claim: Reset tokens have no expiry and are not single-use. Neither function deletes or invalidates the row in `resets` after a successful reset, and neither checks a creation time. A leaked or old token can reset the password again at any later time.
finding.source: A previously issued or leaked reset token for a victim's email, supplied by the attacker as $token.

trace.note: Selects the token by email only, with no expiry column and no used flag.
The token is verified, but nothing records that it has been consumed.
The password is updated and true is returned. The resets row is left in place, so the same token works again.

finding.guards_checked: hash_equals gives a constant-time comparison. There is no deletion or expiry logic anywhere in the file. There is no rate limiting. Any deletion or expiry could exist in the caller or the database schema, which are not in this repo, so this is plausible rather than confirmed.

verdict.guard_found: none (hash_equals at reset.php:14 only compares the token; there is no DELETE/UPDATE on resets, no expiry or used column, and no rate limiting)
verdict.reason: reset.php:13 selects only `token` by email, and neither reset.php:14-17 nor the rest of the file consumes or expires the row, so an old or leaked token can set a new password again. The file is the only code available, so the caller or schema could still delete or expire rows, but nothing here prevents reuse.
